newsitem.title: USA: U.S. balloonist crosses corner of Libya.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist crosses corner of Libya.

text.p: An American balloonist flew over the corner of Libya on Saturday but permission to do so likely came too late for him to be the first person to circle the globe nonstop in a balloon, a mission spokesman said.
Permission for Steve Fossett to fly over Libya was denied early on Friday, forcing him to detour south of the country and out of the most favourable wind currents.
Late on Friday night, the President's Security Council in Libya changed its mind and said Fossett, 52, could go through its airspace, said Alan Blount, a spokesman for mission control in Chicago.
But Blount said it was "doubtful at this point" that Fossett could make it all the way around the world because the change in his route had "taken a lot of fuel and time."
The change in course took Fossett across Chad south of Libya although he did cross the southeastern corner of Libya while his team back in Chicago hoped he could make it to India or beyond.
At 4:30 a.m. EST (1030 GMT) Fossett was over Chad, about 50 miles (80 kms) inside Libya's border, drifting at an altitude of 26,200 feet (7,860 metres).
Project manager Bo Kemper said on Friday India looked like the most logical end point for the journey. If Fossett winds up there he would have made it roughly half way around the world.
"The team and Steve are very disappointed," Kemper told reporters.
"But on the other hand it has been an unbelievably successful trip. Equipment worked 100 percent. The weather was working 100 percent. The only thing that didn't work was political," he said.

The political news came in a three-line telegram from the Libyan government with a terse denial signed "best regards." It ended days of back-channel and public negotiating to win permission for Fossett to use Libyan airspace.

The new route, over Egypt after Niger and Chad, will cause Fossett to use an extra day-and-a-half's worth of fuel, Kemper said. More importantly, he said, the dip south would take him out of the favourable wind current that pushed him across the Atlantic in three days.
"It's like the train is leaving the station without him," Kemper said. "The chances of him recovering (the winds) are negligible."
"It doesn't look good," he added. "It significantly reduces our chances."
The U.S. State Department condemned Libya's refusal to let Fossett cross the country, saying it reflected the "paranoia of the Libyan leadership."
While Kemper refused to call the mission over, he said "The only reason to keep flying will be to break the duration record."
The current mark for time spent in a balloon is six days and 16 minutes set in 1981 by Richard Abruzzo and Troy Bradley. Fossett's trip began late on Monday in St. Louis.

Fossett got the bad news from Libya just after breaking his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 5,435 miles (8,747 km) over Algeria. Kemper set the earlier mark on a voyage from South Korea to Canada.
Libya's hostile relations with the United States left the two countries without formal diplomatic ties.
